utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, this is Case Number IT-94-2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nikolic, good afternoon to you. Are you hearing in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Upawansa Yapa appearing for the Prosecution with Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. David Hackney. Our case manager is Ms. Diana Boles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. Appearances for Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Howard Morrison, lead counsel for Mr. Nikolic, together with Ms. Tanja Radosavljevic as co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, too. So this Status Conference has been convened in accordance and as required by the regulations, by the Rules of this Tribunal, which precisely require that we hold a Status Conference every 120 days to take stock of the situation, and also to ensure the expeditious preparation and adequate preparation for the trial. In addition, also it gives the accused an opportunity to raise any issues that may be appropriate in relation to his physical, mental condition. The agenda of today's Status Conference is relatively a short one, and I propose to start first with pending motions, first of which is a motion filed by the Prosecution last month, in October. And it is Prosecution's Motion for Protective Measures and for a Submission of Corrigendum to Rule 65 ter (E) (i), (ii), and (iii). I think it's appropriate that we take these in order. And I should like to deal first with the motion for the protective measures. There seems to me to be two categories of persons, witnesses, for whom the Prosecution is seeking protective measures. One category includes witnesses that the Prosecution has had an opportunity to talk to already. And it seems that on the basis and more or less simply on the basis of the request or desire to have, to benefit, from some kind of protective measures, protective measures are being sought. And then there is a second category of witnesses who, according to what emerges from the motion itself, Prosecution has not had yet an opportunity to talk to. But as I understand it, by way of a precaution, certain protective measures are being sought. I don't know, Mr. Morrison, if you have anything to say about this before I proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence position is really quite straightforward as far as this motion is concerned. We raise no objection to the matters requested by the OTP insofar as it relates to these proceedings. What I would like to make plain is that we do not at the moment concede the jurisprudence which is argued, neither do we deny it. We take a neutral view on the basis that we may at some point in the future, should there be another motion concerning other witnesses, want to consider the position as far as those witnesses are concerned. Therefore, we don't want to bind ourselves by making any jurisprudential or legal concessions at this stage. But for the purposes of this motion and for the purposes which it's required at this stage, we don't object nor do we intend to file a motion unless ordered to do so, simply to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but still the approach that this Trial Chamber has presided -- Pre-Trial Chamber has presided at the moment. The approach it takes is that a simple filing of a motion for protective measures, even if not opposed, does not necessarily entail an automatic rubber stamping Yes by the Chamber, by the pre-trial Judge who, as I see it, under the Rules has a duty to strike a balance between the interests to protect victims and witnesses on one side, and also the rights of the accused on the other. Now, as it is, I am more concerned with the second category of witnesses that the Prosecution is seeking protective measures for, namely, witnesses that have not yet been contacted for one reason or another. And I am not disputing or contesting or arguing about whatever reasons the Prosecution might have had in not being able or not having contacted these individuals. You may sit down, Mr. Morrison. But I think that it is only fit and proper that before the -- we proceed with a decision, we have more information, an update on the situation, on the part of the Prosecution. In other words, we need to be informed whether -- what attempts have been made so far to approach these persons; secondly, what are the reasons -- whether they are asking for protective measures secondly; and thirdly, what are the reasons on the basis of which you are asking for protective measures. In other words, what appears to be until now as a precautionary measure that you are seeking, and I fully understand that you are doing this in a very responsible way, at the same time, I'm telling you that it is not my intention to proceed with granting any provisional protective measures until I am satisfied that they ought to be in place. And for the time being, however precautionary the approach you are taking may well be, I would rather have more information before I proceed any further. The second thing that I meant to tell you, but now more or less I will modify my approach, considering that there is no opposition or no contest on the part of the Defence, is with regard to the first category. For the future, make it a point to provide more details as a ground for your request for protective measures to be put in place. As I see it, I am not completely satisfied that you have put down what I would consider to be clear, sufficient reasons for putting into place these protective measures. So I reserve the position of this Chamber on this matter, taking into consideration, however, the non-opposition forthcoming from the Defence. Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to make the position absolutely plain, of course, we may ourselves find ourselves in a position where we want to seek protective measures for witnesses, which is the reason why we don't object to the first category. The reason we don't object to the second category is because at the moment we don't know what those witnesses say or might say. It is only when we have some indication of what they might say that we would come back to the Trial Chamber, which is why we reserve the position in the way that we have done without taking, as it were, a preemptive opposition without knowing what we are opposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. The third thing I wanted to make clear is that it seems to me that your motion also contemplates the nondisclosure to the Defence of the names of some of these witnesses. If that is the case, and I would invite you to go through your motion again, to see if this is the case, if that is the case, the -- you will certainly be required to provide more details. But as it is, it is not quite clear to me whether you are also seeking this. According to my legal staff, it seems that the possibility that you are seeking such a protective measure is included. If it's not included, perhaps you could make a statement to that effect here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. I take this opportunity to agree with Your Honour's observations on the granting of protective measures, the principles that apply. We fully understand. We made this application, the motion, out of an abundance of caution in respect of certain witnesses. May I say straight away in respect of the question that Your Honour posed to me just now that we have, in respect of the witnesses, the names of witnesses, disclosed to the Defence all the names of the witnesses. And we would not be seeking permission not to disclose. Disclosure has been made. And in respect of certain portions of the motion, the previous filings, we have indicated that we would be moving for pseudonyms in respect of certain witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And on the other hand, I take it that if my reading of the documents that were filed during the 65 ter (E) meetings, I take it that all the names of the witnesses you intend to produce until now have been disclosed to the Defence. Is that correct, Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I mean, unless there's something we haven't been told, and I doubt that very much in this particular case. As far as we know, all the witnesses' names have been disclosed. But that's a matter which is of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we can move to the -- is there anything else you would like to raise in regard to this pending motion? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, with respect, with respect to the granting of the motion where we have asked for protective measures, the position as I understand now is that they will be granted only after we furnish further information. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two categories, as I tried to explain. I don't foresee or envisage any particular difficulties with regard to the first category, especially having heard the submissions of both parties. With regard to the second category, I would like to know first and foremost whether since the filing of the motion you have succeeded in approaching these witnesses. That's number one. Secondly, whether they seek protective measures, because obviously if they do not seek protective measures, there is no point in maintaining your position and asking for precautionary protective measures. If they seek protective measures, and you know that because you have had a meeting or a contact with these witnesses, then obviously you are asking for protective measures, they will not be any longer precautionary protective measures, but they will be full protective measures for all intents and purposes of law. And therefore, the reasons that you brought forward until now are, for all intents and purposes, worthless, because I would require a specific ad hoc reasons justifying your claim for protective measures to be put in place. I think -- have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as the first category now, I don't think there should be any problems at all. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite clear to us. In respect of the second category, we are in the process of contacting them. As Your Honour was pleased to say, some of them may not require, but we are not in a position to say so now. But if that is the case, we would not be moving for protective measures in respect of those witnesses. But if the others, there are only very few do ask for, we will give the information to the Court, to satisfy Your Honour that the protective measures are indeed needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There's a final point that I would like to make actually now that you are not making it yourselves. Attached to your motion, Mr. Yapa, you also submitted a draft decision in which, inter alia, you are asking that the Nikolic Defence shall not disclose to the media any confidential or non-public materials provided by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: In the draft order that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the draft order that you prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: We prepared the draft order in line with the previous orders that were made by the Chamber. There were two orders that were made. It was in accordance with those orders that these draft orders were prepared, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrison. Does that strike you as normal and acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Make it plain that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you have been given all the names already of the witnesses to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The names that we haven't got from the context of the statements, those are people that - I can say it without fear of embarrassment - we could readily guess who they were simply from the context and the place and the times of the statements. So it's no mystery to the Defence. As far as the nondisclosure is concerned, it would not be our intention in any event to disclose to the public any of the material that's set out in the draft motion. So we don't take any issue with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a draft order 9, save where is directly and specifically necessary for the preparation, presentation of this case, the Nikolic Defence shall not disclose to the public the names, identifying information, or whereabouts of any witness or potential witness identified to them by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: To do otherwise could amount to a contempt of Court whether there was an order or not, and we would be very wary of committing such an act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I'll go through this and if it's the case of coming back to you, Mr. Yapa, to be more precise as to what precautionary measures you are seeking, we will do that. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There is -- then there was - this shouldn't be a problem - submission for a corrigendum to Rule 65 ter (E). I don't think there is anything that needs to be said about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Nothing further to be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Is there anything that you would like to state, Mr. Morrison, with regard to the submission of the prosecution for a corrigendum to Rule 65 ter (E)? I don't think it's the case of anything that needs to be said, but anyway. Shall we proceed to the next point? Issues relating to disclosure. This is very important, as you certainly know. And I propose to take the matter up from where we left it, the last Status Conference that we had, which was in turn a follow-up on the 65 ter meeting of July of this year. I will try and represent to you the five points that -- or four points that were made then. All I'm interested in is to be -- to have a confirmation from you as to what the current situation is. In July, I was informed that the Prosecution had nearly completed its obligation under Rule 66. This was more or less confirmed in the Status Conference of July 2002. My question to the Prosecution is whether now, a few months later, the obligations assumed under Rule 66 have been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: The position is as it was disclosed earlier at the status conference: We have made all the disclosures that are necessary in terms of 66. There is one more statement where we have to provide the translation. That will be done in the course of maybe the coming two or three days. So far as Rule 66 is concerned, I could inform Your Honour that the disclosure is -- barring that disclosure that has to be made, is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree to that, Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the time also, the Prosecution had informed the Trial Chamber that two more statements -- it may not be easy for you to remember now, but two more statements under Rule 66(ii) would soon be disclosed to the Defence. I would imagine that if I use the word "soon," that has been done by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Am I correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It has been done. One other matter, if I may refer to, Your Honour: In the course of contacting some of the witnesses, we came into possession, not that many but certain supplementary information, so we are under a duty to disclose those to the Defence. That we will be doing, again, in the next two or three days' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I saw you nodding, Mr. Morrison. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: This all proceeds upon the basis of having, as it were, confidence in one's opponents, which I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, thank you. And then the Chamber had been informed by the Prosecution at the time, that's in July, that five statements then were still in the process of translation, and once that's ready, it would be made available to the Defence. My question to you is whether the translation has been concluded, and following that, whether these five documents were indeed disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These relate more to Rule 68, if I may...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rule 68 came after. These were -- I take it that these were more in the line of Rule 66. In other words, they couldn't be disclosed until that time because they had not yet been translated. These were five documents. I do not have the details of these five documents, obviously, but I just wanted to know whether they have been disclosed, whether they have been translated and disclosed. If Mr. Morrison's memory is of any help in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: We've had both Rule 66 and Rule 68 material disclosed to us. The last Rule 68 disclosure that I recall was weeks ago. If there has been anything since then, or if there was intended to be any further materials in the intervening period of about two months, then I certainly haven't seen it. So if it's pending or if it's thought that it has been disclosed, that's a matter which ought to be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we can actually deal now straight away, because we have touched on the subject of the application of Rule 68. I take it that more or less the two parties are in agreement that this -- the obligation of the Prosecution under this Rule is being adhered to, and that there may be some further need for future disclosure, which I have reason to believe that the Prosecution will take care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have been -- the Prosecution on our part studiously taking steps to disclose and we are disclosing. In fact, today also we have certain documents, not that many, but we will be handing them over to the Defence today. But we will continue to keep to the obligation under Rule 68. So there may be certain other documents that we have to disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything that either of you would like to raise with regard to the matter of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No. I appreciate the question of disclosure is a continuing obligation on the part of the Prosecution, and plainly all I would ask is that material is disclosed as soon as possible. I appreciate that there is an inevitable delay in material coming to the hands of the Prosecution, it being analysed, and if necessary, interpreted, but to date, I am satisfied that material has reached us in a timely fashion and I have no reason to believe it won't in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next point on the agenda that I intend to touch upon is agreed facts. Now, I have gone through, before coming for this Status Conference, I've gone through the document which the Prosecution filed on the 3rd of October - quite detailed, I must say - namely, its pre-trial brief containing the facts admitted, undisputed, and contested, between the parties. But on the 23rd of July of this year, following the agreement that you had reached amongst yourself during the 65 ter meeting, you promised that you would provide this Chamber with a number of agreed facts which would, of course, not include the core issues which would be -- which would need to be proved in this trial. Do I take it that the document that you filed on the 3rd of October crystallises the position, or is it just your version of what is being agreed and contested?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes. May I, Your Honour, explain as to the process that we undertook. We stipulated to -- we agreed -- the Prosecution decided on certain stipulated facts, and then we presented them to my learned friend. And he responded. We had a meeting, and he responded. And those responses were included in the document that we filed with the pre-trial brief. So in that document, particular document, we have the agreed facts, the disputed facts are in a numerical form indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Morrison, in other words, I take it you are familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Very, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree to everything that is stated here as being either contested or agreed to by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That's correct. The matters which are contested are plainly set out and it's no surprise that what is in fact contested is the core of the indictment. There are peripheral matters which are not contested, and some rather less than peripheral matters which are not contested. There are also some matters which are agreed but in a rather different format than the way they were first put to us by the Prosecution. I think we've reached the position where we have now agreed all that we can without, as it were, prejudicing those issues which must be contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any other facts that you would be agreeing to, apart from what has been -- because this may not be exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It may not be. And the way that I've worked so far is to wait until we are approached by the Prosecution to see -- I do not know and cannot guess all of the material facts they wish to rely upon at trial save and except, of course, those which are evident from the pre-trial brief. We are open and remain open to the possibility of agreeing facts, if they can be agreed without prejudice to my client's interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can you undertake to do this before the trial starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I can only respond to those matters which are put to us by the OTP. I will undertake that if matters are put to us by the OTP, to respond to them as soon as practicable, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any other facts that you would like to put to the Defence by way of possible agreed facts, or do you think that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can stay with what you have here and leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I am very thankful to my learned friend for the observation that he made that, as far as possible on the suggestions that we made, he looked into them and then he made his observations. And we recorded his observations verbatim on the document that we filed. But since he is prepared to consider further on the basis of any suggestions that we make, we will look into further and make any suggestions to him to see whether we can come to agreement on any other facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we can leave it at that. And you'll do that if you come to that conclusion. I don't think there's any point in asking you whether you have anything further to say on this point because you've obviously said what you had to say. Which brings me to perhaps the most important part of this Status Conference agenda of today: Trial date and timetable. You will recall that when you met at the 65 ter meeting way back in July, and when we met the day after, the Status Conference, the idea was hopefully then that the trial would start on the 18th of November. It's obvious to everybody now that it will not be possible for the trial to start on the 18th of November also because there is no Trial Chamber that is available that could start this trial, certainly not until at least one of the ongoing trials comes to an end. I had a long meeting before this Status Conference to see what the possibilities are, and what I can say is that this case is pretty high up in the list of -- order of priorities that the Tribunal has in place for hearing and determination. In other words, it will be, if not the first, certainly amongst the first trials to start as soon as practicable, and as soon as practicable means as soon as there is a Trial Chamber that can take over and start the trial. I do not envisage this to take a long time, and I'm doing my best to ensure that it doesn't take a long time considering, in particular, the length of the detention of the accused so far, which I do not have an intention of prolonging unduly. So my words to you in this regard is that this is being taken care of, and hopefully this trial will commence as soon as there is a Trial Chamber that can be seized of it. Are there any comments or matters that you would like to raise on this matter? Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I think what I'm about to say is eminently predictable. Is there any indication when that might be in terms of calendar date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, as there are two cases or three cases pretty much cooked already, or nearing completion, we are not exactly quite sure which one of two of them in particular will come to an end. But we're probably talking of the first two or three months of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: So if we were to prepare ourselves for a trial starting in, say, March of 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't envisage it's going to take -- I don't envisage it's going to be after spring. I don't envisage. I would say just before spring or early spring. That's what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: My problem, with great respect, I'm not sure when spring starts in Malta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Spring in Malta is roughly ten months a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That's what rather worried me, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we did have floods yesterday. So the idea is -- I have been given an indication that we're probably talking around about March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I have also shown my concern that if it's beyond then, that month, I will start to become seriously concerned about keeping your client any further in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Also obliged for that indication, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is just one of the submissions that I have to make: Because the November 18th trial date, the Prosecution took steps to get ready for trial, and then we were more or less ready for trial by that time. Our one concern is to keep the witnesses informed because there are witnesses not in the area where the incidents took place now, they are distributed all over, so there is a duty on us to keep the witnesses informed as to when it is likely for the trial to commence and keep them ready for the trial. That's one observation that I have to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What I -- the message I wanted to convey is that there are two cases in particular, and this is one of them, that are receiving the utmost attention by the Tribunal - not just by me but by the Tribunal - and they have been placed really high up in the order of priorities. This is one of them. Incidentally, may I remind the -- Mr. Morrison of the decision of this Chamber following your motion for -- motion to vary time limits pursuant to Rule 127. You recall that we had extended the time limit for the filing of your pre-trial brief until the 29th of November. Do I take it that we can reasonably expect the pre-trial brief to be filed by that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The pre-trial brief will be filed by the 29th of November. The only caveat I would have is if there's going to be further material disclosed beyond that, plainly it may be necessary to add an addendum to the pre-trial brief as and when any further material becomes pertinent. But the pre-trial brief as an original document will be filed on or before the 29th of November. Whilst I'm on my feet, the "male captus" motion where the judgement was received on the 9th of October, I have today filed a notice of appeal under Rule 108 dealing with that, the appellate position as far as that motion is concerned. Looking at the time scale, there is a theoretical 90 days in which to file the brief from now. My intention is to file any appellate brief well before that 90-day period expires so that we can reasonably predict and expect that any response from the Prosecution can be received and the matter can go to the Appeals Chamber before spring, which, in England, by and large starts on the 1st of June and ends on about the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll certainly not question your decision to file the appeal under Rule 108 because more or less that is your decision, not mine. And I do not intend to question it or discuss it. But may I ask you if you have looked at... Yes. Have you looked at Rule 72, which deals with preliminary motions, including motions challenging jurisdictions and the right of appeal granted --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- by one of the subrules, one of the paragraphs of that rule in cases of motions challenging jurisdiction? You have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: This was a matter that was raised a long time ago before His Honour Judge Hunt. And it was certainly indicated that this was a matter of such fundamental importance that while there was no judicial determination, that the strong indication was that this was a matter which ought to be subject to appellate consideration if either party wished it to be. That was the indication given at that stage. I haven't got the transcript in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I will not deal with this matter any further because of obvious reasons. But I just wanted to bring to your attention Rule 72 just in case you had not gone into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It's a matter which I've given consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the decision to base your appeal on Rule 108 was a considered option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Only because of the indications which had been given before, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because it may well be there will be no appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If Rule 72 applies, that implies a time limit of 15 days, plus the seven days for certification, and if that is the rule that was applicable, then obviously there would be legal consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm obliged for Your Honour's indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So with this caveat, in case there is an appeal, and of course pending the outcome of such an appeal, if and when, the point to be made is that this trial will start at the first opportunity. Having said this, we try and bring this status conference to an end. Are there any matters of a procedural nature that you would like to raise, Prosecution or Defence? Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I do not think we have -- I'm sorry. I don't think we have any other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Morrison, nothing? Okay. Thank you. Which brings me to the last part of the agenda, the last item on the agenda. I'm required by the rules to inquire on the state of health, physical and mental condition of the accused, as well as his conditions of detention. I will put the question directly. Does Mr. Nikolic have any reason -- or any reason to complain or any submissions to make with regard to any of these issues, that is, his state of health and the conditions of his detention? The microphone, please. Of course, neither of them works.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said on the last occasion, the conditions are good. I can say that I feel relatively good, both psychologically and physically. I do have some minor problems, but they are problems which, of course, would not be of interest for the Trial Chamber. Mr. Morrison helped me deal with my problems. I can say that I feel fairly well for the time being. And as you yourself mentioned, Your Honour noticed, I have been here for quite some time. But anyway, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You wouldn't like to add anything in this regard, Mr. Morrison, in addition to your client's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, No. Plainly an extended period in custody is going to be difficult for anyone to deal with. And it is not a matter of breaching confidence because Mr. Nikolic has just said it himself. He has undergone some problems, and we are hopeful that by talking them through and by seeing the progress which the case is making, he's overcoming them himself without any necessity for any third-party intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So coming to a conclusion, I do not envisage any further significant developments except for establishing the date when this trial will commence. And I anticipate that we should be in a much better position to identify such a date, either by the end of this year or very early next year. And therefore, it will -- it is my intention, if this should be the case, to convene towards the end of January a Pre-Trial Conference. By that time, we would have had the pre-trial brief from Mr. Morrison, more or less the disclosure procedure under 66 and 68 would have been "concluded" - in inverted commas because this is always an ongoing process - and I think that we will need a Pre-Trial Conference round about that time. So be prepared for it. You will be advised of the date in good time. But do anticipate a Pre-Trial Conference towards the end of January. Anything else you would like to raise or mention? So I think we can call it a day. I thank you. And since I won't be seeing any of you before January, I wish you best for the coming festive season. Thank you.
